hpi_details: A 44-year-old man presents with a recently noticed, gradually enlarging painless, heavy, hard testicular lump.
ideas: He thinks the hard spot might just be an old fibrous scar or a clogged gland from a forgotten bicycling injury.
concerns: He is terrified that the hard lump is an advanced cancer that has spread, leaving his young children without a father.
expectations: He hopes to get an urgent ultrasound today and a referral to a specialist so he knows definitively what he is facing.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Testicular Seminoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

A solid intratesticular mass requires prompt scrotal ultrasound, serum tumor markers, and urgent urology referral; suspected testicular cancer is managed with radical inguinal orchiectomy rather than scrotal biopsy.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painless, heavy, hard testicular lump
Key HPI features: a 44-year-old man reports a recently noticed, progressively enlarging painless, hard testicular lump.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Testicular Seminoma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Testicular Seminoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Delaying ultrasound and urology referral for a solid intratesticular mass or performing a scrotal biopsy.
management_principles: Arrange prompt scrotal ultrasound, serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH, and urgent urology referral; discuss fertility preservation before treatment where appropriate.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: UpToDate & National Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines 2026

reference_soap.subjective: A 44-year-old man reports a recently noticed, progressively enlarging painless, hard testicular lump.
reference_soap.objective: Perform scrotal examination and urgent scrotal ultrasound; obtain AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH before definitive treatment.
reference_soap.assessment: Solid intratesticular mass concerning for testicular germ-cell tumor, including seminoma.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange urgent urology assessment. If cancer is suspected, management is radical inguinal orchiectomy rather than scrotal biopsy; discuss sperm banking before treatment when relevant.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Testicular Seminoma
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Testicular Seminoma
Implement evidence-based management plan: Scrotal ultrasound, refer for radical inguinal orchiectomy

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation for patient presenting with painless heavy hard lump in testicle of young male.
red_flags: Sudden severe scrotal pain, nausea, or a high-riding testis (possible torsion)
A firm intratesticular mass or rapidly enlarging swelling requiring urgent ultrasound and urology assessment

must_ask.say: When did you first notice the lump, and has it changed since then?
Is the lump painful or tender when you touch it?
Has the lump been getting bigger, and does it feel hard or heavy?
Have you noticed any weight loss, back pain, or breast tenderness?
Were you ever told you had an undescended testicle as a child, or does testicular cancer run in your family?

history.answer: Doctor, I noticed a hard lump on my right testicle, and it has been feeling heavy.
I first felt it about three weeks ago in the shower, and it has been slowly getting bigger and firmer over time rather than starting suddenly.
It is only on my right testicle itself, not on the left side and not up in my groin.
No, there is no pain at all, even when I touch or press on it.
No, I do not have any pain shooting to my lower belly, groin, or flank.
No, I have never experienced anything like this before.
No, my stomach feels completely fine, with no nausea or vomiting.
The lump stays the same size and does not disappear or shrink when I lie down.
Yes, my right side feels heavy and dragging, especially at the end of the day after standing for hours.
It feels like a hard, firm pebble attached right to the testicle.
No, I have no fever, no burning when I urinate, no need to pee more often, and no discharge.
No, the skin on my scrotum looks normal, with no redness, sores, darkening, or odor.
No, I have not had any injuries down there, and it did not start during heavy exercise or sex.
No, I have not had any swelling under my ears, jaw pain, or mumps.
Both of my testicles have always been in the scrotum, and I never had any surgeries down there as a child.
No, I have not lost weight, my back does not hurt, I have no cough, and my chest has not enlarged or felt sore.
I have been with my wife for 15 years in a monogamous relationship, and I have no new partners.
No, I have never had a urinary catheter, bladder scope, or prostate procedure.
We had our two children without any difficulty, and I do not have diabetes or any immune problems.
I looked up hard testicular lumps on the internet, and I am worried it might be testicular cancer.
I'm terrified that this rock-hard lump is cancer that's spreading, and I won't be around to watch my kids grow up.
I'm hoping to get an ultrasound done today and a direct referral to a specialist so I can know for sure what's going on.
I have no chronic medical conditions, no high blood pressure, and no diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers on the weekend.
I work as an office manager and live at home with my wife and two kids.
There is no family history of testicular cancer or any other major health issues.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-appearing male in no acute distress, sitting comfortably on the examination table.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
No gynecomastia, breast tenderness, or palpable breast nodules.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly.
Right testis has a non-tender, firm, solid intratesticular mass that does not transilluminate; left testis and bilateral epididymides are normal.
No inguinal hernia with cough impulse, no varicocele, and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.
